sections.history: Kamakhya crowns Nilachal Hill on the south bank of the Brahmaputra, in the land the old texts call Kamarupa. It is named in the Ashtadasha Shakti Peetha stotram as 'Kamarupe Kamakhya', and later Shakta literature such as the Kalika Purana and the Yogini Tantra makes the hill a centre of Tantric worship. Kings of the region are remembered as its patrons, though the temple's early history is hazy. Tradition says an earlier shrine fell into ruin, with sources blaming different invasions and dates. The present temple was raised in 1565 by the Koch king Nara Narayana, whose brother Chilarai oversaw the work, rebuilding on the remains of a stone temple said to be older. The Ahom kings who followed enriched the complex with new shrines, halls and inscriptions, and it has remained a living centre of worship ever since.
sections.architecture: The sanctum is unlike any other in India. Visitors descend steep steps to a dark chamber below ground level, where there is no sculpted image, only a cleft in the rock shaped like a yoni, kept moist by a spring that never runs dry. Above it rises a tall dome, polygonal and beehive-like, built of brick over a stone base on a cross-shaped plan. This blending of the northern Nagara tradition with a hemispherical Assamese dome is called the Nilachal style, after the hill. A succession of halls leads to the cave, ending in the natmandir, a performance hall with an apsidal, shell-shaped roof from the Ahom period. Around the hill stand smaller shrines of the ten Mahavidyas, the great goddess forms, many with the low curved roofs known as chala.
sections.legends: The legend belongs to the story of Sati. After she gave up her life at her father Daksha's sacrifice, a grief-stricken Shiva carried her body across the world, and Vishnu's discus scattered it so that the earth itself became her body. At Kamakhya, tradition says, her yoni fell upon Nilachal Hill and turned to stone, and the goddess is said to dwell in that rock. The Kalika Purana adds that Kamadeva, the god of desire, reduced to ashes by Shiva, found his form restored here through her grace; hence the land is called Kamarupa, 'the shape of desire'. Her Bhairava is Umananda, honoured on the river island just below the hill. Kamakhya is the goddess as the source of all creation, worshipped here in her creative power.
sections.festivals: The great festival is Ambubachi Mela, held in mid-June at the onset of the monsoon, when the goddess is said to undergo her annual menstruation. The doors close for three days and ritual worship pauses, then reopen on the fourth, when the sanctum is purified and devotees receive sacred water and a piece of red cloth as prasad. Durga Puja is a fortnight-long observance known here as Pakhua Puja, and in the month of Shravana comes the three-day Manasa Puja, with the Deodhani dance. Basanti Puja and Pohan Biya, the goddess's marriage day, are also kept. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the lunar calendar.
sections.experience: Come early and expect a pilgrimage rather than a quiet visit, since the queues for the cave can be long, especially on weekends and festival days, and the paid fast-track lines exist for that reason. Climb the hill, or take the road, and the city falls away beneath you, with the Brahmaputra glinting far below. Many devotees offer red hibiscus and a length of red cloth before going down into the sanctum. In the dim, damp cave the encounter is intimate: the goddess is touched with water, flowers and silence. Afterwards, walk among the Mahavidya shrines on the hill, and consider crossing the river to Umananda on its island.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning, about 5:30 a.m., with a midday closing and a second session in the afternoon until the evening; sources differ, so confirm timings with the temple authorities, especially during Ambubachi and festivals.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside, and many devotees bring red hibiscus, flowers and a red cloth as offerings.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum and inner halls, and rules on phones and cameras within the complex are set by the temple authorities. Check the notices at the entrance and ask before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Kamakhya stands on Nilachal Hill in western Guwahati, about 8 km from Guwahati railway station, with Kamakhya railway station also in the city. Lokpriya Gopinath Bordoloi International Airport lies roughly 20 km away. Taxis and buses climb to the temple, and staircases rise from the foot of the hill for those who prefer to walk.
